pos: n. (frozen vapour falling in white flakes; the Bible's standard of whiteness; rendering Hebrew sheleg, Greek chion)
etymology: From the Saxon snaw, cognate with the Latin nix, nivis. In Palestine snow is uncommon at low elevations and permanent on Hermon, which is why Scripture treats it as a marvel and a measure rather than as a nuisance.
biblical_def: Snow in Scripture is the standard of whiteness, and it is used where sin is being dealt with. Isaiah's great invitation is the chief instance: “Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool” (Isaiah 1:18). Two things deserve notice. God summons the guilty to reason rather than merely to submit, and the colour named is scarlet — a dye that does not wash out. The promise is not that the stain will fade but that it will be replaced by its opposite. David asks for the same thing as a personal mercy: “Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Psalm 51:7) — hyssop being the bunch used to apply blood at the passover and in the cleansing of a leper, so the whiteness is asked for on sacrificial grounds. At the tomb the angel's raiment is “white as snow” (Matthew 28:3), the colour of heaven appearing at the resurrection. And Proverbs uses snow to name a thing out of season: “As snow in summer, and as rain in harvest, so honour is not seemly for a fool” (Proverbs 26:1) — not impossible, but wrong, and damaging to the crop.
webster_summary: Frozen vapour, and Scripture's measure of white. Isaiah offers to make scarlet sins as snow; David asks to be washed whiter than it; and Proverbs makes snow in summer the picture of honour given a fool.
webster_full: SNOW, n. [Sax. snaw; L. nix, nivis.] Frozen vapor; watery particles congealed by cold in the air, and falling in flakes.
2. Figuratively, whiteness or purity; as, white as snow.
3. SNOW, v.i. To fall in snow; as, it snows.
4. SNOWY, a. White like snow; as snowy raiment.
5. In Scripture, an emblem of purity and of pardon; though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be white as snow, Is. 1.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 1:18 is quoted as though God's pardon were a simple amnesty, detached from the sacrifice that grounds it and from the repentance the chapter demands three verses earlier.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 1:18 is one of the most quoted verses in the Bible and one of the most commonly amputated. Two verses before it God has told the same people to wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes; cease to do evil; learn to do well, and two verses after it he says that if they refuse and rebel they shall be devoured with the sword. The invitation to be made white as snow is issued to a nation whose hands were full of blood, and it is issued with both a summons to repent and a warning attached. Preaching that keeps the snow and drops the scarlet, the repentance, and the alternative has turned a covenant lawsuit into a greeting card.

The principle to recover is what makes the whitening possible. David does not ask to be washed whiter than snow on the ground of his sincerity; he asks to be purged with hyssop, the instrument that applied blood. Scarlet was a fast dye and no scrubbing removed it, which is exactly why the promise is astonishing. Sin is not rinsed out by amendment of life; it is covered and answered by a substitute, and the whiteness afterward is real because the death was real. Revelation completes the picture with a paradox no other religion could write — robes made white in the blood of the Lamb (Revelation 7:14).
roots_summary: Hebrew sheleg is snow, and the verb shalag, to be snowy. Greek chion is snow; leukos, white, is the colour it measures.

pos: n. (frozen rain falling in stones; a standing instrument of divine judgment; rendering Hebrew barad, Greek chalaza)
etymology: From the Saxon hagal. The English word is a homonym of the greeting hail (from Old Norse heill, health), which is unrelated; the weather word is a Germanic term for the ice that falls in stones.
biblical_def: Hail is the weapon Scripture reaches for when God fights from the sky. It is the seventh plague on Egypt: “the LORD sent thunder and hail, and the fire ran along upon the ground; and the LORD rained hail upon the land of Egypt” (Exodus 9:23) — and the account is careful to note that Goshen had none, so that the storm distinguished between peoples. It fights for Israel at Bethhoron: “the LORD cast down great stones from heaven upon them unto Azekah, and they died: they were more which died with hailstones than they whom the children of Israel slew with the sword” (Joshua 10:11). The tally is stated deliberately — God killed more of the enemy than the army did, on a day when Israel was doing everything right. Isaiah makes it the destroyer of false security: “the hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies, and the waters shall overflow the hiding place” (Isaiah 28:17), in a passage where the true foundation is the tried stone laid in Zion. And Revelation gives the last hailstorm: “there fell upon men a great hail out of heaven, every stone about the weight of a talent: and men blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail” (Revelation 16:21). Under a judgment that plain, men still cursed — which is Scripture's standing answer to the notion that sufficient evidence produces repentance.
webster_summary: Frozen rain in stones, and Scripture's weapon from the sky. It falls on Egypt and spares Goshen, kills more at Bethhoron than the sword, sweeps away the refuge of lies — and in Revelation is cursed rather than heeded.
webster_full: HAIL, n. [Sax. hagal.] Masses or particles of ice falling from the clouds, usually in showers, and generally in warm weather.
2. HAIL, v.i. To pour down particles of ice, or frozen vapors.
3. HAILSTONE, n. A single mass or particle of ice falling from a cloud.
4. In Scripture, an instrument of divine judgment; the hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies, Is. 28.
5. HAIL, exclam. [Sax. hal, whole, sound.] A term of salutation, expressive of a wish for health; a distinct word.
corruption_summary: Natural judgments are treated as purely meteorological, so that Scripture's claim that God governs storms is set aside — while Revelation 16 quietly refutes the belief that clearer evidence would produce faith.
corruption_paragraphs: The instinct of the age is that weather is weather and that any theological reading of it is superstition. Scripture's claim is not that every storm is a judgment, and Christian prudence should be slow to assign meaning to particular disasters — our Lord expressly refused that reasoning about the tower of Siloam (Luke 13:4). But Scripture does claim that God governs the weather absolutely and that he has used it in judgment by name and on the record. The plague on Egypt was announced in advance, spared Goshen precisely, and stopped when Moses spread his hands. That is not weather with a moral gloss added; it is a stated act with a stated purpose, and the alternative is to treat the narrative as fiction.

The principle to recover is Revelation 16:21, which is the most important verse in Scripture about the limits of evidence. Hailstones of a talent weight fall out of heaven, the plague is unmistakable, and the recorded human response is blasphemy. Men did not lack proof; they lacked a new heart. This is why the Reformed doctrine of total depravity is not pessimism about human behaviour but realism about the will: the natural man does not fail to believe because the case is thin, and no display of power has ever converted anyone. The Spirit gives sight, or the brightest evidence is only better-lit darkness.

pos: n. (a violent disturbance of the air; figuratively, sudden calamity; rendering Hebrew saar and sufah, Greek lailaps)
etymology: From the Saxon storm, akin to stir. Hebrew saar is a tempest or whirlwind, from a root meaning to sweep away; the same word describes the whirlwind that took Elijah up and the wind that God rides.
biblical_def: A storm in Scripture is never merely weather, because the God who made the wind is always in the sentence. The Psalter states the government plainly: “He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still” (Psalm 107:29) — part of a psalm about men who go down to the sea in ships and see the works of the LORD in the deep. Nahum states the harder half: “The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet” (Nahum 1:3). He is not merely master of the storm; the storm is his road, and the clouds are what his walking kicks up. Isaiah adds the pastoral use: God is “a strength to the poor, a strength to the needy in his distress, a refuge from the storm, a shadow from the heat, when the blast of the terrible ones is as a storm against the wall” (Isaiah 25:4) — the storm here being the violence of powerful men, and the shelter being God himself rather than a change in circumstances. Mark records the disciples' night: “there arose a great storm of wind, and the waves beat into the ship, so that it was now full” (Mark 4:37), and the Lord was asleep in the hinder part on a pillow. The rebuke he gave was to the wind and then to them.
webster_summary: Violent disturbance of the air. Scripture makes God its master, its rider, and the refuge from it — he maketh the storm a calm, has his way in the whirlwind, and is himself the shelter from the blast.
webster_full: STORM, n. [Sax. storm.] A violent wind; a tempest. Thus a storm of wind, is correct language, as the proper sense of the word is rushing, violence.
2. A violent assault on a fortified place; a furious attempt to take a fort by scaling the walls.
3. Violence; vehemence; tumult; commotion; as a storm of angry passions.
4. Adversity; calamity; distress; affliction.
5. STORM, v.i. To raise a tempest; also, to rage; to be in a violent agitation of passion.
corruption_summary: God is made the rescuer from storms but not their ruler, so that calamity is treated as outside his government — which spares him blame at the cost of the only comfort actually on offer.
corruption_paragraphs: A widespread pastoral instinct, and the formal doctrine of open theism behind much of it, protects God's goodness by limiting his control: he did not send the storm, he only helps in it. The relief is momentary and the cost is total. If the wind is outside his hand, then no promise about it is worth anything, and Psalm 107:29 becomes a hope rather than a fact. Open theism (Pinnock, Boyd, Sanders) denies exhaustive divine foreknowledge and thereby denies the God of Scripture, who declares the end from the beginning and says my counsel shall stand. Nahum 1:3 refuses the escape route in the same breath as it comforts: the LORD is slow to anger, great in power, will not acquit the wicked, and hath his way in the whirlwind. His goodness and his government are asserted together or not at all.

The principle to recover is what happened in the hinder part of the ship. The disciples' question was not canst thou save us but carest thou not that we perish — the accusation was against his love, not his power, which is usually the case. He stilled the wind first and then asked why they were so fearful, how is it that ye have no faith? The storm was not evidence of his indifference; his sleeping in it was evidence of his authority over it, and their terror was a failure to reason from the Person in the boat to the wind outside it.

pos: a. (of the colour of growing herbage; living, fresh, unseasoned; rendering Hebrew yaraq and raanan, Greek chloros)
etymology: From the Saxon grene, from growan, to grow — the colour is named directly from growth. Hebrew raanan means luxuriant or flourishing, and is applied both to a righteous man and to the tree under which idolatry was practised.
biblical_def: Green in Scripture means alive and growing, and it is used with more edge than the pleasant colour suggests. Its sweetest use is the shepherd psalm: “He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters” (Psalm 23:2) — and the verb is causative, maketh me, because sheep do not lie down while hungry or afraid. Mark preserves an eyewitness detail at the feeding of the five thousand: the Lord “commanded them to make all sit down by companies upon the green grass” (Mark 6:39), which fixes the season and shows a shepherd seating a flock in a green pasture. But the Psalter also uses green of the wicked: “I have seen the wicked in great power, and spreading himself like a green bay tree” (Psalm 37:35) — flourishing, well-rooted, and the next verse says he passed away and could not be found. Greenness is not evidence of righteousness. The most solemn use is our Lord's, spoken to the women weeping as he was led out: “For if they do these things in a green tree, what shall be done in the dry?” (Luke 23:31). Green wood does not burn easily; dry wood does. If God did not spare the living, fruitful, innocent One when he stood in the sinner's place, what shall become of the dead and barren who stand in their own?
webster_summary: The colour of growth, and so of life. Green pastures are the shepherd's gift; a green bay tree is the flourishing of the wicked; and the green tree of Luke 23:31 is Christ, from whom judgment argues to the dry.
webster_full: GREEN, a. [Sax. grene, from growan, to grow.] Of the color of herbage and plants when growing; verdant.
2. New; fresh; recent; as a green wound.
3. Fresh; flourishing; undecayed; as a green old age.
4. Not dry; containing its natural juices; as green wood; green timber.
5. GREEN, n. The color of growing plants; also, a grassy plain or plat.
corruption_summary: Visible flourishing is taken as proof of God's favour, though the Psalter uses green expressly of the prospering wicked — and Luke 23:31 is seldom pressed to its terrible conclusion.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 37:35 exists to prevent an inference everyone is tempted to draw. The wicked man is not withering; he is in great power and spreading like a well-watered native tree, and the psalmist says he saw it — the observation is granted, not denied. What the psalm adds is time: he passed away, and lo, he was not; I sought him, but he could not be found. Prosperity theology cannot survive contact with this psalm, and neither can the quieter version of it that measures a ministry, a family, or a nation by present greenness. Scripture's counsel is mark the perfect man, and behold the upright: for the end of that man is peace — and the operative word is end.

The principle to recover is the arithmetic of Luke 23:31. Our Lord tells the daughters of Jerusalem not to weep for him but for themselves and their children, and gives this reason: if the Romans do such things to a green tree, what will be done to a dry one. He is the green tree — living, fruitful, without sin — and he is being burned. The argument runs from the greater to the lesser and it is meant to terrify: if the sword awoke against the Shepherd, the man that is God's fellow, no dry branch will be spared on the ground of its own condition. The only shelter is to be found in the green tree rather than beside it.

pos: n. (a creature of the waters; rendering Hebrew dag, Greek ichthus and opsarion)
etymology: From the Saxon fisc, cognate with the Latin piscis. The Greek ichthus became the earliest Christian emblem, its letters taken as an acrostic for Jesus Christ, God's Son, Saviour — a sign scratched where a cross would have been dangerous.
biblical_def: Fish enter Scripture under man's dominion in the creation mandate: “let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth” (Genesis 1:26). The order given to Adam covers the water before it covers anything else. God then uses a fish as an instrument of both judgment and rescue: “Now the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights” (Jonah 1:17) — the verb is prepared, and our Lord took those three days as the only sign that would be given his generation. In the Gospels fish are the ordinary food that Christ multiplies: “We have here but five loaves, and two fishes” (Matthew 14:17), a boy's lunch out of which a hillside was fed. And after the resurrection, John counts them: Peter “drew the net to land full of great fishes, an hundred and fifty and three: and for all there were so many, yet was not the net broken” (John 21:11). The number is exact because the man who wrote it counted them on a beach at daybreak, and the unbroken net is noted because on an earlier morning, before the cross, the net had broken (Luke 5:6). The risen Christ's draught holds.
webster_summary: Creatures of the waters, under man's dominion from Genesis 1. A prepared fish holds Jonah three days — the sign Christ claimed — and the risen Lord's draught fills a net that does not break.
webster_full: FISH, n. [Sax. fisc; L. piscis.] An animal that lives in water. Fish is a general name for an animal that swims and breathes by gills.
2. The flesh of fish, used as food.
3. FISH, v.i. To attempt to catch fish; to be employed in taking fish.
4. To seek to obtain by artifice, or indirectly; as, to fish for compliments.
5. In Scripture, the fish of the sea are given to man's dominion, Gen. 1; and fishers of men, Matt. 4.
corruption_summary: The dominion given in Genesis 1 is read either as a licence to exploit or as an embarrassment to be apologised for, when Scripture makes it a stewardship exercised under God and answerable to him.
corruption_paragraphs: Two readings of the creation mandate both go wrong. The first takes dominion as ownership and treats the creatures as raw material with no claim of any kind — a reading Scripture contradicts by requiring the ox to rest on the sabbath, forbidding the muzzling of the treading ox, and commending the righteous man who regardeth the life of his beast. The second reading, embarrassed by dominion, effectively denies the ordering of Genesis 1 and puts man among the creatures rather than over them, which cannot be squared with a text that makes only man the image of God. The biblical position is stewardship: real authority, really delegated, and answerable at a real accounting. A steward may use what he manages and may not waste it.

The principle to recover is the sign of Jonah. Our Lord staked his identity on a fish story that modern scholarship has often treated as folklore, and he did so in the plainest terms: as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth (Matthew 12:40). He also said the men of Nineveh would rise in judgment against his hearers because they repented at Jonah's preaching. Both statements assume the events happened. To read Jonah as a parable is not a neutral literary judgment; it removes the sign Christ pointed to when he was asked for evidence.

pos: n. pl. (birds; the winged creatures of the air; rendering Hebrew oph, Greek peteinon)
etymology: From the Saxon fugel, a bird — the general Germanic word for any flying creature, later narrowed in English to domestic poultry. In the KJV it keeps the wide old sense: every bird is a fowl.
biblical_def: Fowls in the Authorized Version are birds of every kind, made on the fifth day: “Let the waters bring forth abundantly the moving creature that hath life, and fowl that may fly above the earth in the open firmament of heaven” (Genesis 1:20). Our Lord draws his best-known argument against anxiety from them: “Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they?” (Matthew 6:26). The reasoning is from the lesser to the greater and it turns on a relation — not God feeds birds merely, but your heavenly Father. Birds are fed by a Creator; disciples are fed by a Father. But Scripture does not sentimentalise them. In the covenant scene of Genesis 15, “when the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away” (Genesis 15:11) — a long, strange afternoon of guarding split animals from scavengers before God passed between the pieces alone. And in the parable of the sower the fowls are the enemy: “some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up” (Matthew 13:4), which the Lord interprets as the wicked one catching away what was sown in the heart. The same creature that preaches providence also pictures the theft of the word.
webster_summary: Birds, in the KJV's wide old sense. Christ makes them the argument against anxiety — your heavenly Father feedeth them — while Genesis 15 and the parable of the sower show them as scavengers and as the snatching away of the word.
webster_full: FOWL, n. [Sax. fugel.] A flying or winged animal; the generic name of certain animals that move through the air by the aid of wings.
2. It is used as a collective noun; as, we dined on fish and fowl.
3. In common usage, a domestic cock or hen.
4. FOWL, v.i. To catch or kill wild fowls for game or food.
5. In Scripture, the fowls of the air, all birds; behold the fowls of the air, Matt. 6.
corruption_summary: Matthew 6:26 is reduced to a general reassurance that things work out, detached from the Fatherhood it rests on — and from the labour Scripture everywhere assumes the anxious man should still be doing.
corruption_paragraphs: Two things are usually lost in the popular use of this verse. First, the ground of the comfort is a relationship, not an observation about nature. Birds are fed by their Creator; the promise our Lord makes is to those who can say your heavenly Father, and it belongs to those who seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness. Offered indiscriminately, the verse becomes a general optimism that experience will eventually contradict. Second, the argument is not against work. Birds do not sow or reap, but no bird sits still — they are busy from first light, and the passage forbids anxious care rather than diligence. Scripture in the same breath commends the ant and condemns the sluggard.

The principle to recover is that the fowls carry two lessons and the church usually remembers one. In Matthew 13:4 they descend on seed sown by the wayside, and the Lord names them: then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart. Every congregation contains hearers whose hearing is stolen before the service ends. Abram's afternoon in Genesis 15 is the practical answer — he drove them away, hour after hour, until the sun went down and God passed between the pieces. Guarding what has been sown is ordinary, unglamorous work, and it must be done by hand.
roots_summary: Hebrew oph is winged creatures collectively, from uph, to fly. Greek peteinon is a flying thing; ornis is a bird, used of the hen gathering her chickens.
roots_lines: Hebrew oph (H5775) — fowl, winged creatures; from uph, to fly.

Hebrew ayit (H5861) — a bird of prey, a screamer; the fowls that came down on Abram's carcases.

pos: a. (untamed; growing without cultivation; ungoverned; rendering Hebrew pere and sadeh, Greek agrios)
etymology: From the Saxon wilde, untamed. Hebrew pere is the wild ass of the desert, a byword for an animal that will not be harnessed; sadeh means of the field, and so uncultivated.
biblical_def: Wild in Scripture means untamed and uncultivated, and it is applied to men as readily as to animals. The angel's word about Ishmael is the sharpest instance: “he will be a wild man; his hand will be against every man, and every man's hand against him” (Genesis 16:12) — literally a wild-ass of a man, free, ungovernable, and at odds with all. Hosea turns the same figure against Israel: they “are gone up to Assyria, a wild ass alone by himself: Ephraim hath hired lovers” (Hosea 8:9). The picture is of a nation that mistook independence for strength and ended up buying the affection it would not receive by covenant. Mark uses the word of our Lord's temptation: “he was there in the wilderness forty days, tempted of Satan; and was with the wild beasts; and the angels ministered unto him” (Mark 1:13) — the second Adam in a wilderness rather than a garden, among beasts that were no longer at peace with man. Paul's use is the most important, because it is where the reader stands: “thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree” (Romans 11:17). Gentile Christians are cuttings from an uncultivated tree, grafted into a cultivated root against nature, and told a few verses later not to boast.
webster_summary: Untamed, uncultivated. Ishmael is a wild man, Ephraim a wild ass alone, the second Adam is among wild beasts — and the Gentile believer is a wild olive branch grafted in, and warned not to boast.
webster_full: WILD, a. [Sax. wilde.] Roving; wandering; inhabiting the forest or open field; hence, not tamed or domesticated; as a wild boar; a wild ox.
2. Growing without culture; as wild parsnip; wild cherry.
3. Desert; not inhabited; as a wild forest.
4. Savage; uncivilized; not refined by culture; as the wild natives of Africa or America.
5. Ungoverned; licentious; inordinate; as wild passions; wild mirth.
corruption_summary: Wildness is romanticised as authenticity, and untamed independence is preached as strength — the very posture Hosea calls a wild ass alone by himself, hiring lovers.
corruption_paragraphs: A great deal of modern encouragement, including in Christian books, urges men to recover something wild — to be untamed, unmanageable, and free of the constraints that have supposedly domesticated them. Scripture uses the image and reaches the opposite verdict. The wild man of Genesis 16 lives with his hand against every man; the wild ass of Hosea 8 is alone by himself and reduced to hiring the loyalty he had by covenant and despised. What Scripture commends is not tameness in the sense of timidity but a will broken to God's and set to work: the meek inherit the earth, and the fruit of the Spirit ends with temperance, which is the Spirit's own word for a strength under government.

The principle to recover is Romans 11:17 and the warning attached to it. A wild olive branch is worthless as a producer; grafting normally runs the other way, cultivated scion into hardy root, and Paul knows he is describing something contrary to nature. That is the point. Gentile believers were the uncultivated stock, brought in by mercy alone and partaking of a fatness they did not grow. Paul's application is immediate and severe: boast not against the branches… thou bearest not the root, but the root thee. Every branch that thinks its standing is owed to its own quality has forgotten which tree it came off.
roots_summary: Hebrew pere is the wild ass; sadeh, of the field, uncultivated. Greek agrios is wild, of the field; agrielaios is the wild olive of Romans 11.

Of the Gentile branch grafted in: thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them (Romans 11:17).

And if some of the branches be broken off, and thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree;

pos: n. and a. (the abyss of waters; that which is far below; rendering Hebrew tehom, Greek bathos and abussos)
etymology: From the Saxon deop. Hebrew tehom is the primeval deep, the mass of waters over which the Spirit moved — a word used absolutely, without an article, as a proper name for the great abyss.
biblical_def: The deep is one of the Bible's first nouns: “And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters” (Genesis 1:2). The unformed waters are not a rival power God must subdue — the surrounding nations told that story and Genesis does not — but material he has made and over which his Spirit broods. At the flood the deep is unsealed: “the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened” (Genesis 7:11), water coming from beneath and above at once, so that the judgment undoes the second and third days of creation in reverse order. The Psalter uses it for the depth of affliction: “Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me” (Psalm 42:7) — and the psalm insists twice more that the sufferer shall yet praise him. And our Lord commands a fisherman into it: “Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught” (Luke 5:4), after a night of nothing. Peter's objection and obedience are both recorded — we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word — and the catch that followed put him on his face.
webster_summary: The abyss of waters. The Spirit broods over it at creation, its fountains break up at the flood, it is the Psalter's word for affliction, and Christ commands a discouraged fisherman to launch out into it.
webster_full: DEEP, a. [Sax. deop.] Extending or being far below the surface; descending far downward; profound; opposed to shallow.
2. Low in situation; being or descending far below the adjacent land.
3. Not superficial or obvious; hidden; secret; as a deep design.
4. DEEP, n. The sea; the abyss of waters; the ocean.
5. That which is profound, not easily fathomed, or incomprehensible; as the deep things of God, 1 Cor. 2.
corruption_summary: Genesis 1:2 is read through the myths of surrounding nations, so that the deep becomes a chaos-monster God defeats — which makes creation a struggle rather than a sovereign word.
corruption_paragraphs: Comparative readings of Genesis 1 frequently place tehom alongside the Babylonian Tiamat and conclude that Israel inherited a combat myth in which the creator subdues a hostile sea. The text will not carry it. There is no battle in Genesis 1, no adversary, and no struggle — there is a Spirit brooding and a God speaking, and the deep does what it is told. Where later poetry does use the imagery of the sea being rebuked, it is precisely as a display of unopposed sovereignty. The doctrinal stake is high: if creation involved a contest, then God's power is a matter of degree rather than kind, and creation out of nothing goes with it. Genesis 1:1-2 asserts that only God is uncreated, and everything else, the deep included, is his work.

The principle to recover is Luke 5:4 as a pattern for obedience. Peter is a professional who has just worked all night in those waters and has the strongest possible evidence that the fishing is bad. Christ's command is against his expertise, at the wrong time of day, and in the deep water where nets are hardest to handle. His answer — nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net — is a complete theology of obedience in nine words: the objection is stated honestly, and the word of Christ outranks it. What follows is not merely a catch but a man on his knees saying depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord.
roots_summary: Hebrew tehom is the primeval deep, the abyss of waters; metsulah is the depths of the sea. Greek bathos is depth; abussos, the bottomless place.

pos: n. (the land bordering the sea; the strand; rendering Hebrew choph and saphah, Greek aigialos)
etymology: From the Saxon score, probably from sceran, to shear or cut — the line where the land is cut off by the water. Hebrew saphah is a lip or edge, so the sea shore is literally the sea's lip.
biblical_def: The shore is where land meets sea, and Scripture uses it for two things: the sand that measures a promise, and the standing-place of Christ. God's oath to Abraham after Moriah fixes the first: “in blessing I will bless thee, and in multiplying I will multiply thy seed as the stars of the heaven, and as the sand which is upon the sea shore” (Genesis 22:17). Hebrews takes up the same measure and adds the wonder of it — that from one man, “and him as good as dead, so many as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as the sand which is by the sea shore innumerable” (Hebrews 11:12). The shore is the standing image of a number no one can count, given to a childless man. In the Gospels the shore is where the Lord stands to teach and to meet his own. Pressed by crowds, “he went into a ship, and sat; and the whole multitude stood on the shore” (Matthew 13:2), and from that boat came the parables of the kingdom. And after the resurrection: “when the morning was now come, Jesus stood on the shore: but the disciples knew not that it was Jesus” (John 21:4). They had gone back to fishing and caught nothing; he was already on the beach with a fire of coals and bread, waiting for men who did not recognise him. The shore is where the risen Christ meets returning failures with breakfast.
webster_summary: Where land meets sea — in Hebrew, the sea's lip. Its sand measures the promise given a childless man; and it is where Christ sat to teach the parables, and stood at daybreak to feed disciples who had gone back to their nets.
webster_full: SHORE, n. [Sax. score, from sceran, to shear or cut off.] The coast or land adjacent to the ocean or sea, or to a large lake or river.
2. This word is applied primarily to the land contiguous to water; but it is used for the ground within the flux and reflux of the tide.
3. SHORE, n. A prop; a buttress; something that supports a building.
4. SHORE, v.t. To support by a post or buttress; to prop.
5. In Scripture, the sand which is upon the sea shore, an emblem of number innumerable, Gen. 22.
corruption_summary: The Abrahamic promise is spiritualised until it means nothing in particular, or narrowed to a single ethnic line — when Paul makes the seed Christ and the heirs all who are of faith.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors handle this promise badly. The first empties it, treating the sand and stars as poetry with no definite fulfilment, so that God's oath after Moriah becomes a warm sentiment. The second narrows it to physical descent alone, which is the assumption behind the dispensational scheme that keeps Israel and the church on permanently separate tracks — a framework unknown to any Reformation confession. Paul settles the sense of the promise in Galatians: the seed is Christ, and if ye be Christ's, then are ye Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise (Galatians 3:16, 29). The innumerable multitude of Revelation 7, out of every nation and kindred and people and tongue, is the sand of the sea shore counted.

The principle to recover is the shore of John 21. The disciples had returned to their old trade, fished all night, and taken nothing — and the risen Lord was standing on the beach in the half-light with a fire already lit. He does not begin with rebuke; he asks whether they have any meat, tells them where to cast, and feeds them. The restoration of Peter follows breakfast rather than preceding it. Christians who have gone back to something they left, and are ashamed of the night's catch, should know who is usually standing on the shore at daybreak.
roots_summary: Hebrew choph is a coast or haven; saphah is a lip, and so the shore of the sea. Greek aigialos is a beach or strand.

Greek aigialos (G123) — a beach, strand, shore; where the multitude stood and where Christ stood.

pos: n. (a body of land surrounded by water; in the KJV also isle; rendering Hebrew i, Greek nesos)
etymology: From the Saxon igland, water-land; the intrusive s was added later by false association with the unrelated isle, from Latin insula. Hebrew i means a coastland or island, and in the prophets stands for the distant maritime nations.
biblical_def: An island in Scripture is a place at the edge of the known world, and the Bible's interest in islands is chiefly that the gospel reaches them. Luke, a careful traveller, names them as they pass: “running under a certain island which is called Clauda, we had much work to come by the boat” (Acts 27:16), and after the wreck, “when they were escaped, then they knew that the island was called Melita” (Acts 28:1). On that island a viper fastened on Paul's hand, the islanders changed their minds about him twice, and the father of the chief man was healed — a shipwreck turned into a mission. John writes Revelation from one: “I John… was in the isle that is called Patmos, for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ” (Revelation 1:9). A prisoner on a rock in the Aegean received the vision of the throne, which is a permanent comment on where God does his largest work. And the islands appear at the end: “the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together; and every mountain and island were moved out of their places” (Revelation 6:14). The most fixed things men know — mountains and islands, the very definition of permanence to a sailor — are moved. Isaiah had promised long before that the isles should wait for God's law.
webster_summary: Land surrounded by water, and in Scripture the edge of the known world. Paul is wrecked on one and heals there; John receives Revelation on one; and at the end every island is moved out of its place.
webster_full: ISLAND, n. i'land. [Sax. igland, water-land; the s is an intruder from the unrelated isle.] A tract of land surrounded by water.
2. A large mass of floating ice is called an island of ice.
3. ISLE, n. ile. [L. insula.] An island; a tract of land surrounded by water.
4. ISLANDER, n. An inhabitant of an island.
5. In Scripture, the isles, the maritime countries and distant coasts; the isles shall wait for his law, Is. 42.
corruption_summary: Isolation is treated as exile from usefulness — a believer set aside by circumstance assumed to be out of God's service — when Patmos produced Revelation and a shipwreck produced a mission.
corruption_paragraphs: The instinct that God's work happens at centres, in front of crowds, and in seasons of freedom is very hard to shake, and it leaves Christians in confined circumstances concluding that their useful years are over. Scripture's record is otherwise with monotonous regularity. Joseph in a prison, Daniel in a foreign court, Paul in chains writing to Philippi, John on a rock — the confinements are where much of the Bible was produced. John states plainly why he was there: for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ. The island was a punishment intended to silence him, and it is the address from which the church received its vision of the throne, the Lamb, and the city.

The principle to recover is Melita. A ship breaks up, a prisoner swims ashore among strangers, and what follows is a fire of sticks, a snake, a healing, and three months of hospitality that ended with the whole island provisioning the voyage. None of it was planned by Paul, and all of it was providence. Christians whose plans have come apart in a storm should read Acts 28 slowly. The Lord had told Paul in Acts 27 that he must be brought before Caesar; getting there involved a wreck, and the wreck was not a detour from the mission but part of it.
roots_summary: Hebrew i is an island or coastland, used in the prophets for the distant maritime nations. Greek nesos is an island; nesion, a small island.
roots_lines: Hebrew i (H339) — an island, a coastland; the isles that shall wait for his law, Isaiah 42:4.
Hebrew choph (H2348) — a coast or haven; often paired with the isles in prophetic geography.
Greek nesos (G3520) — an island; Melita, Patmos, and the islands moved in Revelation 6:14.
Greek nesion (G3519) — a small island; Clauda, under which the ship ran in Acts 27:16.
Greek naugeo (G3489) — to suffer shipwreck; Paul's repeated experience, 2 Corinthians 11:25.
usage: Of the wreck that became a mission: they knew that the island was called Melita (Acts 28:1).
Of a prisoner given the Revelation: was in the isle that is called Patmos, for the word of God (Revelation 1:9).
